subsubtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ANNUAL ESCALATION OF PENSIONS OF MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES AND MOUNTED POLICE-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because this is an urgent matter I ask leave under the provisions of Standing Order 43, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) to move:
That this House urges the President of the Treasury Board to introduce at an early date the necessary amendments to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act so that retired Canadian Armed Forces and Royal Canadian Mounted Police personnel will have their pensions escalated annually, in accordance with the rise in the cost of living, commencing in the year following the year of retirement, regardless of age, thus ending the unfair discrimination which applies to many such personnel.

speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the right hon. Prime Minister. It arises out of the continuing discussion on rules governing Crown corporations. Given the fact that it seems that one of the major reasons for some of the great difficulties in which Crown corporations are now finding themselves is that boards of directors are not fulfilling their obligations as well as they might, does the government plan to inform all directors whom they appoint to Crown corporations that they have responsibilities to fulfil as least as great as those specified under the Canadian Corporations Act?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is with respect to the Polysar matter and in view of the fact that the truth of the matter came to light not particularly as a result of effective government controls but rather from vague and random government processes, if even that.
Would the Prime Minister take steps to give the Public Accounts Committee the authority and the staff necessary to make a full investigation of all government controlled corporations, including the power to examine all board minutes, supply contracts and other like documents, which have been denied to the committee thus far in its investigation of the AECL matter? I ask that question particularly in view of the fact that in the cases of both Crown corporations which have been investigated by this committee thus far business practices have been revealed which charitably can only be described as slipshod.

The House will recall that the action which was taken resulted in an assertion and statement being made by independent auditors and lawyers that there was nothing untoward in the actions of Polysar. It was only later that a subsequent inquiry came out with a contrary opinion, and perhaps the committee of the House will be trying to reconcile these two contradictory opinions.
As far as the suggestion of the hon. member is concerned, if it is just enjoining the committee to do everything it can to get to the bottom of this, I would support the desire of the hon. member. However, if he is suggesting that the committee be given special powers, and they are not within the traditions of our parliamentary system, I suggest that this is a matter for the House to decide. If the House wants to make a special reference to that committee, perhaps the hon. member can discuss that with the government House leader, with whom he has daily contact.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Has the minister caused an investigation to be made as to the truth of the allegation regarding this leak? If not, I hope he will. Will he also advise the House why Statistics Canada found it necessary to hide some 300,000 people who should have been in the statistics relating to unemployment?

The House resumed, from Monday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-22, to amend the statute law relating to income tax, be read the third time and to pass.
Mr, Speaker, last Monday 1 made a few remarks in the House regarding Bill C-22-

Order.

February 14, 1977
Income Tax

-and since that time many things have happened. I think it is only fair that I declare a conflict. The hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) presented me with a can of hard candy which she said were humbugs. I want to declare that in no way will I be swayed by the corporate sector in this House with respect to the discussion of Bill C-22. The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) says they are jawbreakers. 1 do not know. I have had a few of them, and I think that they were meant to sweeten my personality.
Hear, hear!

I hear the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale). He was pretty loud on Monday night. As the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader, he had the responsibility for organizing the timing of this debate in the House. If I was speaking for a few hours last Monday, it is his fault in the House and he has to accept the responsibility.
Oh, oh!
I would have far preferred him to have stood and accepted responsibility for the mistake he made, and 1 would be prepared to forgive him for having made it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There was no mistake, John.

I hear shouts across the aisle from the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne). He said I was delaying the House and I was preventing the taxpayers of Canada from getting their rebates. In looking at the hon. member's riding, I see he will get $800,000 under the Canada Works program. That means the unemployment rate must be pretty high in his riding. I wish he would stand in the House and I wish he had stood at the report stage of the bill and spoken about unemployment in his riding. But all he can do is make remarks from behind the curtain across the way.
It is only fair to deal with whether the taxpayers of Canada would be delayed in receiving their rebates, if they have rebates coming to them. On checking with Revenue Canada, I find the following statistics show that National Revenue processed only 3 per cent of all tax returns by mid-March, and this bill will come to a vote long before we get to that stage of the game. But what is more significant, we on this side of the House argue that tax rebates can take place without the passage of this bill. After all, we had the example of Bill C-21.
I see the hon. member nodding in recognition of this.
That legislation dealt with excise tax legislation appeals and sales tax exemptions. It relates to the same May budget. It has been administered by the Department of National Revenue as if the bill had been passed.
To nail down this argument and once and for all to put it to rest, I want to put some figures on the record. Figures from the Department of National Revenue show that by mid-March 1.9 per cent of returns on taxable income were processed, and 5.5 per cent on non-taxable, for a total average of 3 per cent.

By mid-April 17.5 per cent taxable and 27.5 per cent non-taxable were processed and the total average was 20.2 per cent. By mid-June 33.1 per cent taxable and 43.6 per cent non-taxable were processed and the total average was 36 per cent. By mid-August the figure for taxable had jumped to 89 per cent, and 95.2 per cent for non-taxable, and the total average was 92.3 per cent. By mid-November, 98 per cent of all returns had been processed by the Department of National Revenue.
I bring these figures to the attention of the House to lay very effectively to rest the criticism which came from the benches opposite and from those to my right that our careful examination of Bill C-22 has somehow denied or delayed the taxpayers of Canada getting their rebates. As these figures show, Canadians waiting for rebates have not been jeopardized in any way.
I will be dealing with that matter again, but one thing which has really struck me is the time we have spent on this bill. All the provisions of Bill C-22 were mentioned in the May, 1976, budget. We have to keep the timetable in mind because it demonstrates very clearly that the allegation that we on this side of the House have delayed the bill is incorrect. It is alleged that we have embarrassed the government and that we are trying to obstruct parliament.
Never.

I know we never obstruct parliament. Parliament will not be obstructed by the 16 members of the New Democratic Party or by one little school teacher from the backwoods of northern Ontario. If that should happen, God help democracy in Canada.
Hear, hear!

As I said, all the provisions of this bill were mentioned in the May, 1976 budget. When was first reading of this bill? November 5, 1976. The government says it is concerned about the taxpayers of Canada; it says it is concerned about rebates. But when did we start second reading of the bill? December 2, 1976. When we came back after the Christmas holidays, what was the first item for parliament to debate? Radio and television in the House. I see the hon. member for Assiniboia banging his desk like a seal flipping his flippers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You voted for it.
I wish a couple of ministers would throw him a fish.
He would throw it back.

If he kept it, he might get mercury poisoning. What are the priorities of this government? I recognize the importance of radio and television in the House. I recognize it even more since last Monday. It would have been wonderful to have had radio and television in the House, because we could have taken this show right across Canada, to
February 14, 1977

the embarrassment of the government which is so incompetent and incapable of administering its own legislation.
Hear, hear!

All we asked for was ten hours to look at the clauses of Bill C-22 in some detail. Instead, we spent 7'h hours on Monday and 2'h hours on a closure motion debate. Today we will use four hours to consider this bill. When we add it up, we get nine hours.
Would it not have been easier and much more productive for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the government House leader to have agreed with the New Democratic Party and permitted ten hours of debate on the clauses of Bill C-22? It seems to me that we on this side of the House are very reasonable people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It seems to you.

The hon. member had his chance to make a speech. He deferred, so I am taking his time. His idea of democracy is that all debate is unreasonable. I recall the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) in the committee in the old days. He never wanted discussion of any bills at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Have you ever been to the Saskatchewan legislature? You should see how Blakeney operates.

We are reasonable people and we are quite prepared to discuss these things. All we asked for was ten hours to look at this legislation. Much has been said about our wasting time, taking up parliament's time, and all the rest of it, but I sat in this House and listened to unending debate on gun control which took months and months. Then it went to committee, and it still has not come back to parliament. That was a waste of time. We spent seven months debating capital punishment in this House. So for members of the government or members to my right to say that the New Democratic Party is filibustering or wasting time is not being fair at all. We have tried to give considerable and detailed examination to the provisions of Bill C-22. We have kept completely open minds. We have no axe to grind.
Something else happened since last Monday. People across Canada started to respond and I think it is only fair for me to mention some of those people who responded. There was a response from Elliot Lake. I received a telegram which says: "Congratulations, John. Kick them in the "-" ankles. It is from Roy and Evelyn Raftery of Elliot Lake. Here is another one from Sudbury. This one says: "Dear John, Give them hell". That is from Phil Landry, Mick Lowe and residence. Here is one from the boys from Bay Street. It says: "Congratulations ... on behalf of vast majority of Canadians and incidentally all teachers. Don't forget AIB. Keep it up." It is from Frank, Doug and Pat, the boys from Bay Street. I do not have many friends on Bay Street. As a matter of fact, there are only three of them, and I hope to make their acquaintance.
Here is a telegram from Winnipeg: "No more tax concessions for corporations and the wealthy. Keep up the fight".

That is from Jim Durcan. Here is one from Capreol, Ontario, where I live. It says: "You may have done something to change the rubber-stamp image of parliament". That is from Catherine M. Gilbert. Keep that in mind. Here is one that I am very proud of:
Best wishes. Local is proud of representation provided constituents of Nickel Belt which our members worked and elected you. It is gratifying that the Sudbury region has a spokesman for the wage earners and the unfortunates of Canada. It is unfortunate the Liberals or Tories have not the quality of members in the House they portrayed to the voters during an election. Our union's voice is with you.
That is signed, "Dave Paterson, President, local 6500, United Steel Workers of America." Mr. Speaker, that is the largest local of union members in all Canada, with some 16,000 hourly-rated employees. Here is one that really throws the lie in the teeth of any member across the way. I hope the hon. member for Assiniboia is listening. He was yelling across the floor the other day, "They want their RRSPs". Here is a letter that touches the heart:
Mr. Rodriguez, keep up the work. I will gain if the bill passes, but I would rather give up the gain to give the break to the old aged or the underpaid.
It is signed, "Josie Budnick".
There are a few benevolent people in this country.
The hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan) on a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
Would the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) permit a question from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance?
Certainly. Any time, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, has the hon. member received any telephone calls, letters or telegrams asking him to sit down?

No, Mr. Speaker. Since this started last Monday I have found what a wellspring is within the Canadian heart. When you get letters such as that last one, you know you are on the right track. When people across the country are prepared to say, "I stand to gain from this thing, but the things you have said are very important," we ought to take a good, hard look at them. The hon. member can yap and ask all the questions he wants. Here is an example. On Monday I got up and made my few remarks in a humble-
Oh, oh!

-and sincere way to the House. Lo and behold, in the Toronto Star of February 8, alongside the story covering what I said in the House is an article headed, "Ottawa to close income tax loophole in retirement plans".

February 14, 1977
Income Tax
This is a Canadian Press article. I hope hon. members are listening, because I want to put it on the record. It reads as follows:
Federal tax investigators say they are cracking down on taxpayers using loopholes in registered retirement savings plans to avoid millions of dollars in income tax every year.
They knew it all along.
A Revenue Canada official said in an interview, the department is about to pounce on several hundred persons who have been using a wrinkle in the law.
But in the case of a second savings incentive program-registered home ownership plans-he said an unknown number of persons have used the plan as a tax dodge.
This is done simply by changing ownership of the home they already own over to the spouse's name. Both loopholes were created in November, 1974, when John Turner, then minister of finance-
He is the man who went to his eternal reward in the bosom of Bay Street.
They should have put closure on the loopholes.
That is right, but we never seem to be able to catch those loopholes.
Or the minister.

The article continues:
-introduced changes in regulations to permit establishment of retirement savings plans on behalf of spouses.
At the same time, he created the registered home ownership plans "to assist young people in accumulating the capital required for a down payment on a house."
Both savings programs are vigorously promoted by chartered banks and trust companies at this time of year because deposits must be paid into the plans by March 1 in order that the amount of the deposits may be deducted from last year's taxable income.
For most people, the maximum amount that may be deposited in a registered retirement savings plan-commonly called a RRSP-is $3,500.
The money is taxable only when it is withdrawn from the plan. The theory is that the money will be withdrawn only in later years when a person is retired and therefore subject to a lower tax rate.
When the government introduced "spousal" plans in 1974, some taxpayers began to engage in what the revenue department considers sham transactions. Typically, these sham transactions work this way-
These are what we call the loopholes in the plan. That is what we on this side of the House are against. It is really the crux of the whole thing. Here was an opportunity for a minister who really felt that the country should be supported by the taxes collected from those who had earned from the society and ought to be paying their fair share of taxes. Surely a tax plan is not to be set up so that every Tom, Dick and Harry, his dog and cat, can climb through the loopholes. I hope the minister is thinking about what I am saying. Here are the loopholes, according to this article:
The husband, the highest earner and therefore the highest taxed partner in a marriage, deposits $3,500 in a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP). He does this in his wife's name and before the March 1 deadline.
The husband deducts the $3,500 from his 1976 taxable income.
Shortly after the March 1 deadline, the wife-who is in a lower tax bracket- cashes in the RRSP and reports the money as taxable income for the current year, 1977.
[Mr. Rodriguez.)
This technique, merely a way of transferring income into a lower tax bracket, can be repeated year after year.
"There's a fair number of people who have done it," the revenue department official said.
"We're going after a few hundred, and serving notice on everyone that we're going to stop letting them play games."
How nice, Mr. Speaker! As the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) says, of course the trust companies, banks and insurance companies are going to report them. You can just see it. It is too ludicrous. Let some low income earner who is on unemployment insurance take out of the unemployment insurance fund something that he is not entitled to, and then see how he is tracked down. He can never escape: everything but bloodhounds are put on his track. This is the kind of loophole that we want to discuss and bring home to this government again and again. Something has to be done to plug that loophole. The income tax system must have credibility for the large number of Canadians who pay taxes. If people see that it has no credibility, they lose faith in the democratic process. That affects what we are doing in this House. We have to try to bring that home to the government.
The hon. member for York Centre wants to know if people have asked me to sit down. Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to stand here and talk until doomsday if that is what it will take to bring home to the Minister of Finance that something is seriously wrong with the system. That is only one loophole, but there are others in Bill C-22 that we want to discuss. As long ago as April, 1976, the minister was made aware of this loophole and urged in a meaningful way to block it. Mr. Speaker, an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of April 13, 1976, succinctly and clearly pointed out one of the loopholes in our law, a loophole which still exists in Bill C-22. The article read:
A few readers expressed mild annoyance that editorials on this page recently criticized illegitimate but nonetheless legal ways to avoid personal income taxes without giving enough detail on how to cash in on the bonanzas, in question.
They weren't just joking, either. They really didn't see why a minority of taxpayers should exploit tax laws in ways that weren't intended to be used but which are not prohibited by law. The Journal doesn't see why, either-but since giving detailed financial advice isn't one of the functions of editorials, the "how-to" details on tax dodges will have to be found elsewhere.
But some advice can and should be given. It's for the federal government. If a particular method of tax avoidance is considered an "abuse" of the tax laws, don't wait for more and more taxpayers to commit the act before cracking down on it.
If no change in the law is necessary to prevent fast "rollovers" of tax-free cash between husbands and wives under the guise of a registered retirement savings plan, for instance, then make it clear with a stern announcement.
Spell out what kinds of transactions qualify a taxpayer for the $1,000 interest income deduction from taxable income. If a quick buy-and-sell trade with bonds is considered an abuse, then explain exactly how long such securities would have to be held to qualify the taxpayer for the legitimate deduction.
Where Revenue Canada frowns on a tax avoidance device but is powerless to stop it because of the way the law is written, it should put pressure on the finance department for the necessary changes in law to close loopholes. The government should announce ahead of time its intention to make such changes. This would be a comfort to the majority of taxpayers who don't use loopholes and a useful service to the expanding minority who are being lured into them by the government's apparent laxity.
February 14, 1977

The need for clarification was well expressed in a recent brief to the Minister of National Revenue by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business:
The Journal quoted part of that brief as follows:
When the department remains silent on how it will treat certain flawed sections that can be easily abused, uncertainty and cynicism on the part of the majority of taxpayers who wish to be fair is the result.
The article went on to say:
If there is one thing Canada doesn't need more of, it's uncertainty and cynicism about the tax system. The government faces a massive job of cleaning up the incredible obscurity left over from tax reform that took effect in 1972. But the kinds of loopholes at issue here-such as in the RRSP, investment income deductions and the registered home ownership savings plan-are more recent imperfect creations than tax reform. They are also easier to tidy up in the interests of fairness and a healthier public attitude toward taxation. That job should be done now.
To that we say "Amen". That job should be done now. It is obvious to anyone reading the clauses of Bill C-22 and noting the existing loopholes that the theme of the bill is "one good loophole deserves another." The loopholes are legion. Considering that the provisions of Bill C-22 were mentioned in the budget of May, 1976, surely the Minister of Finance, together with his parliamentary assistants and nabobs in the bureaucracy, has had sufficient time to consider these loopholes and move effectively to block them. I do not blame the Minister of National Revenue (Miss B6gin), for the responsibility lies with the Minister of Finance. In this connection I cannot help noting another article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of November 27, 1976, entitled "An ounce of cure." The article reads as follows:
Revenue Canada has let it be known that, among others, a tax dodge called the quick bond trade is under intense scrutiny and that taxpayers found to have used it will be pursued. The aim is apparently not to punish but to recover funds lost to the government under the device and to discourage its use in future. But it's almost a token exercise.
The quick bond trade usually works this way: Persons with less than the allowable $1,000 in tax-free interest or dividends arrange to buy and sell a bond simultaneously, acquiring accumulated bond interest that is tax free. The cost of the transaction, including the accumulated interest they bought from the previous bondholder, is tax deductible.
The attraction of the deal is obvious. Someone might acquire $1,000 in instant tax-free income while the $1,060 or so that it cost to acquire the income is reduced by the amount of the taxpayer's marginal tax rate. For someone in the 45 per cent bracket, for instance, the net cost of acquiring the $1,000 would be about $585, leaving a profit of more than $400 at the expense of other taxpayers. This could be done every year.
The weakness of Revenue Canada's campaign against this abuse is the limitation of the tax law. It can be used against "sham transactions" in which it is clear that no money changes hands, but it's doubtful whether it will prevent the same deal being carried out over a short period in which real money is put at risk. Since some bonds can be bought with little short-term risk for only four per cent down, the slightly less quick bond trade will still be wide open to abuse.
This, sad to say, is the problem with several other tax loopholes that should be closed. Revenue Canada is working to foil a significant number of taxpayers, for instance, who set up registered retirement savings plans for their low-or-no income spouses and then collapse the plans immediately to obtain a tax saving. But the loophole will apparently still remain for those with the small patience to allow a decent interval before skinning the taxman for the same amount.
The most effective place to crack down on tax loopholes is at their source. The source is the finance department, not the revenue department. Under the guise of stimulating savings through tax incentives, the government through the finance department devised too many abuse-prone tax laws. The revenue department's watchdog efforts may serve only to cause determined tax-avoiders to use more discretion. The impact on the millions of dollars lost annually in tax collections may be minimal.
Income Tax
I point out that the articles I have quoted from this afternoon came into my possession as a result of events which took place last Monday evening. People concerned about the direction in which our country is heading, and the cynicism prevalent in our government, sent this material to me pointing out those further loopholes as evident in the material which I have placed on record this afternoon. Last Monday evening, toward the end of my remarks, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) stood up and asked a question. He asked: What is the model for our tax system? That is a fair question, considering we are discussing a bill with such implications for the Canadian taxpayer. My model is the model of this party, the New Democratic Party: we believe there are three basic principles to a tax system under a socialist government. First, the tax system ought to be redistributive. There is no question about that. In this regard, the Carter Commission stated, in volume 1 of its report, page 6:
We are firmly convinced that this redistribution is necessary if we are to achieve greater equality of opportunity for all Canadians and make it possible for those with little economic power to obtain a decent standard of living.
That is our first principle, that the system must be redistributive. Not even a Tory would quarrel with that. But that principle would have to be accepted on all sides of the House. The second principle in our tax model is equity. I again wish to refer to the comments of the Carter Commission, volume 1, page 4:
The first and most essential purpose of taxation is to share the burden of the state fairly among all individuals and families. Unless the allocation of the burden is generally accepted as fair, the social and political fabric of a country is weakened and can be destroyed.
We know that is happening today. There are grave disparities between the bottom one-fifth of the Canadian population who every year receive a smaller percentage of the economic pie while those at the top receive a greater percentage. It was certainly neither fair nor realistic for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to stand on January 26 and say he does not care if the rich in this country get richer as long as the poor get richer. He was obviously speaking in a vacuum. He does not realize the implications of the spread within the Canadian economic system. What has happened to the just society? Did it dissipate like dew in the early morning sun? We no longer hear much about the just society.
The third factor in our tax model is progressivity. I cannot stress that enough: the system must be progressive. Therefore, the three principles are redistribution, equitability and progressivity. It must be imposed on a broad base which embraces practically all forms of income and wealth. We are not alone in this position: it is not an isolated position. The Carter commission buttresses the principle of progressivity. I quote from page 272 of volume 2:
The greater the income, the greater should be the relative net contribution of the family or individual.
We do not have a progressive income system. The government knows full well that every time it comes in with a program or indexing exemptions, a registered retirement sav-

February 14, 1977
Income Tax
ings plan, a surtax or a child care allowance based on a formula dependent on income, it destroys the concept of progressivity. The higher up the income scale you are lucky enough to be, the greater the advantage with these kinds of programs. We fall into the trap of saying that all Canadians who are working and earning a wage can take advantage of the registered retirement savings plan, the registered home ownership savings plan or any of the other 18 loopholes in the system. However, we know full well that those at the bottom of the scale could never afford to take advantage of that sort of program.
We see a model with three principles. Our model is based upon the principle of ability to pay. There must be equality in tax treatment between men and women and between persons in like circumstances. I cannot stress that enough. Our model is based on reducing the gap between the rich and the poor by greater reliance on progressive, direct taxes on income and wealth. We have pleaded with successive Liberal and Tory governments to ensure progressivity in the tax system by using tax credits. We harp on that time and again. However, we do not get anywhere. We have not gained one inch in getting them to move toward a system of tax credits which would be the forerunner of a guaranteed annual income in this country.
That would be one of the best ways of eliminating poverty for over one-quarter of our people, 5 million Canadians, who live below the poverty line. What a travesty of our traditions, with so many living in poverty! Every time members go to the parliamentary restaurant they enjoy scrumptuous meals at cut rate prices, subsidized by the taxpayers of Canada. They should be asking themselves whether there is anything that can be done in this House to make the tax system fair and just.
Last Monday I suggested-and there were howls from the other side of the House-that when one looks at the income tax system in Canada one cannot help being impressed by the obvious close consultation between the wealthy in Canada and those who sit on the government benches. When I threw that out there was a whole slew of catcalls and howls.

The suggestion I made in this House is not as far out as some may think. Do they really touch their lives at all? A lot of the clauses in the bill, as I have pointed out before, do not really touch the lives of the large majority of our people. It seems to us on this side of the House that only a small minority are able to take advantage of tax programs such as RRSP, RHOSP and the elimination of the surtax on those with incomes of over $30,000.

We in this party have argued consistently that the legislation which is outlined in Bill C-22 is regressive in nature. One of the principal reasons for saying this is that Bill C-22 increases the tax deferrals and loopholes and adds to the numerous subsidies already present in the Income Tax Act which are largely beneficial to the wealthy and affluent. It is a deliberate deviation from the principle of progressivity. It is a primary deviation from the principle of equity, Mr. Speaker. It deviates from the principle of redistribution which we have talked about as our model for an income tax program in Canada.
The clauses on child care, registered savings plans, registered retirement savings plans, disabled persons and the registered home ownership savings program are inequitable in their application since they always give greater benefit to those at the top of the income scale than to lower income groups. As well, they are absolutely of no benefit to the poor who are outside the tax system because their incomes are too low. These deductions and deferrals must be reviewed in the light of more information that has come to my attention.
Hon. members on the government side keep on repeating that we have a fair taxation system and that the fiscal benefits we have been discussing do not unduly favour high income earners at the expense of low wage earners. Government statistics are impressive. Indeed we have been told that the vast majority of taxpayers who benefit from those deductions belong to the group of people at the bottom of the income scale. They continuously put forward impressive statistics

which show, they say, that most fiscal benefits go to those who earn less than $10,000 a year. But statistics, Mr. Speaker, do not always tell the truth.
It reminds me of the story of a statistician. I believe he used to work for the Department of Finance and he once wanted to cross a river but did not know how deep it was. Looking up available statistics, he learned that it was three feet deep on average. As a statistician of the Department of Finance, he thought that information was quite enough. And, Mr. Speaker, do you know what happened to him? He drowned. His own statistics misled him, just as the Canadian taxpayer is misled by the statistics given to him by the government. Yes, the average depth of the river was three feet; but, Mr. Speaker, in some spots it was two feet, in others, five and even eight feet; and that is where we lost our statistician.
Mr. Speaker, we do not want Canadians to suffer the same fate. Unfortunately, just like the statistician who worked for him, the Minister of Finance allows himself to be misled by statistics that do not always tell the whole story. The minister tells us that 77 per cent of deductions allowed for child care go to families whose income is less than $10,000. The government likes to quote such striking figures. We do not question their accuracy. But those same figures hide the truth. That is, that in terms of dollars, child care allowances are more profitable to Canadians in high income than in lower income brackets.
The National Welfare Council, in its report entitled "The Hidden Welfare System" states as follows:
A deduction always gives a greater benefit to the person with a higher income and a lesser benefit to a person with lower income. This is because deductions always take money out of a person's highest tax bracket-the bracket which is taxed at the highest rate applicable to his income.
Of course, we are not opposed to increases in child care allowances. But we are opposed to a tax system that provides for a considerably higher tax savings to the taxpayer who can best afford to pay the expense, and consequently has less urgent need of the subsidy afforded by the tax system. Deductions always give that type of results. The higher the deduction, the greater the disparity.
The National Council of Welfare gives us an example which shows how tax savings accrued from this deduction are much higher for the well-off than for the low income taxpayers. It illustrates how a person with an income of $6,000 a year, who is eligible for the child care deduction would save $257 whereas a person with an annual income of $20,000 would save $380 in tax with the same basic exemption. This is a good example of the type of situation the present government is hiding with its impressive statistics. This is the same kind of situation which made our statistician drown. We have a tax saving of $257 for the low income earner and one of $380 for the upper income taxpayer; is this what the government calls a fair tax system?
If we really had a fair tax system, as stated by this government, could they explain why in 1974 there were 252 citizens with an income of over $50,000 who did not pay any tax, and among them 17 had an income of over $200,000? Could they give us an explanation as to why the gap between the wealthy

Amendments like the child care deductions tend to reinforce inequality, to maintain if not increase the gap between high income and low income groups. Our alternative is to replace this unfair child care deduction system by a tax credit system. Let me quote the Canadian Council of Welfare report; it says:
The way to eliminate this inequity is to replace the child care deduction with a child care credit.
When fiscal allowances are socially justified, as is the case for child care allowances, they should benefit equally all wage earners, and this can only be achieved by fixed tax abatement system. Tax abatement is the best way to distribute the national income. This has nothing of a revolutionary idea. Some provincial governments use them to finance social programs. The federal government is well aware of the way these tax abatements are used. In fact, they are working very well as far as election expenses deductions are concerned. There are a great number of well-off benefactors who are friends of our Liberal and Progressive Conservative colleagues and who are well aware of the value and advantages of this particular use of the tax deduction system. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we could at least take a first step towards a fairer Canadian tax system if the Liberal would be as concerned about the financial condition of the individual taxpayer as they are about the financial position of their own party.
If the government really believes, as it says it does, in a fair tax system, it will implement a tax credit system where it is required, particularly in the area of financial assistance to child care expenses, care of elderly and disabled people, as well as a variety of other important social programs. One of the benefits provided by the tax credit system is to ensure the payment of tax on every dollar earned. Now, I understand this might be a horrifying thought for a Liberal government and their Progressive Conservative friends who would be greatly alarmed by the loss of loopholes in such an advantageous tax legislation. They will certainly create dissatisfaction among their friends from the big industry. However, it is a measure of which the other 95 per cent of our people might take advantage.
Bill C-22 is unfair. It grants higher deductions to those at the top of the income scale. Take corporations, for instance. The higher corporate tax is not paid by the rich. The share of all revenues paid by corporations to the tax system has rapidly decreased during the past few years. From 1962 to 1970, corporate contributions to federal revenue have decreased by some 38 per cent whereas the contributions paid under personal income tax have gone up by over 23 per cent.
Not only are those Canadians who are in the lower 20 per cent income bracket becoming poorer every day but they carry a heavier tax burden. In the main, the tax system does not assist at all in redistributing incomes in Canada and Bill C-22, with amendments such as clause 21, relating to deductions for child care, emphasized even more the unfairness of the Canadian tax system.

As I stated, the child care deduction always gives greater benefit to the person with a higher income and lesser benefit to the person with a lower income. This is because deductions are always taken out of a person's highest tax bracket, the bracket which is taxed at the highest rate applicable to his income. The way to eliminate this-and this is documented by the National Council on Welfare-is to replace the child care deduction with a child care credit. A tax credit is just what its name implies, a credit of a fixed amount which each taxpayer could apply against his or her tax bill; in other words, a fixed amount of tax which he or she would not have to pay.
How is it possible to have that kind of tax credit with respect to election expenses and contributions? How is it possible to have that sort of tax credit applied to contributions to a political party? To me, that is a very fair way to go about it; but if we can do it in politics, why is it not possible to do it with respect to child care? They can no longer say that a direct tax credit is not workable, because it was that Liberal gang over there which used to tell us on this side that a direct tax credit would never work. But suddenly they needed party funds, and lo and behold, up pops a tax credit. Yes, we voted for it because we felt that any contribution to a political party should be above-board. We said, "No more handing over of envelopes in boardrooms. No more trips down to 10, Toronto street." No, sir, all contributions to political parties should be above-board, we believe. We do not object to that, but by the same token we believe that with regard to child care allowances there should be a direct tax credit and it should be above-board so that everybody sees where your hands are and nothing is done under table. Surely that principle should carry over. What gets to me is that in the House we have the power to do that. We can allow a direct tax credit to people who have to work and support a child. The child care reduction was replaced by a credit of $350. Women earning $6,000 and women earning $20,000 would receive the same fixed amount.
But the minister says that screws up the percentages.

The actual tax dollars are not applied in a fair manner. The minister may have figures about how nicely these dollars are distributed in percentages. He may say that 60 per cent of the people take advantage of the child care allowance, but how much is that in dollars and cents? That is what we on this side are interested in. The minister keeps giving us percentage figures, but we are talking about how much that is in tax. Cuanto dinero, is what we ask. That is important. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) says "Si si". That is true. That is the response we have had in the House to tax credits. That is what we want to see. On top of all this, the child care clause is discriminatory, which I am sure the hon. member fo Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) will never be able to understand. At least he may live to regret his words. I do not have to deal with him any longer; that has all been taken care of.

Someone, perhaps Anne Dea of Edmonton who's an Alberta representative on the federal Advisory Council on the Status of Women, should tell MP Marcel Lambert (PC-Edmonton West) the facts about the role of women in the last quarter of the twentieth century.
Lambert, objecting to income tax amendments that would raise the amounts working parents can deduct for child care costs, was complaining that women go to work for frills, not out of economic necessity.

As for the 2,303,000 married women in the work force, they aren't working for frills either. They're working because, in many areas of this country, it takes two incomes in a family to pay off the mortgage on a house. Some of those married women have alcoholic husbands, or unemployed or disabled husbands; without their earnings, these families would be on welfare.
Lambert opined, too, that children sent to day care centres become social monsters.
This would come as a great surprise to child welfare workers, for example, who find day care centres an excellent way of rescuing children from the risk of being neglected or abused by their parents.

Dear Sirs:
Re: Income Tax Act, S. 63, Child Care Expenses.
The Child Care Expenses section contains other discriminatory aspects which should be investigated and corrected.
1)	The policy of this section is unacceptable since it assumes a woman must shoulder the child care responsibility. She must bear the expense of the babysitter when she goes out to work in the paid labour force. Women generally earn 60 per cent of men's incomes. (Statistics Canada, Dept, of Labour, Women's Bureau). Thus either her husband pays for child care and she deducts it (which is unfair to the husband, who should be able to deduct his real expenses). Or, she pays the expenses (usually more than the permitted deduction) and her earning power and consequently her financial independence is considerably reduced. This sex-stereotyped division of responsibilities is especially discriminatory. A clause should be developed which allows for maximum flexibility of responsibility and/or joint responsibility.
2)	An indirect discrimination results from the absence in the definition of child care expenses (S 63 (3)(a)(ii)) of persons studying in full-time institutions. Under "earned income" there should be added a provincial or Canada loan or grant. 3)	The $1,000 per child is inadequate and unrealistic in terms of the present cost of living and cut-back wages. A person running a business is entitled to deduct the full amount of expenses. 4)	The child care expense deduction should be from tax payable-

What about incentive?

You should have told him about your case.

from home to home. In the February, 1977, issue there is an article entitled "Your money-how happy marriages can pay off in real cash at tax time", by William Scott. The article reads:
She's a wonderful woman, your wife. But now there's some even better news. She's more wonderful than you realized-she's worth money to you. Real, hard cash that you can put in your pocket.
It's all thanks to the government, which has devised a number of nice tax advantages for the married couple. Yet surprisingly, few married couples take advantage of the breaks available.
Don't just think of her as friend, companion, lover, and helpmate. She also could be the best tax shelter known to man.
Most of the tax advantages available to the married man flow from a sharing of property.
The hon. member says he knows that. He designed the tax system and he stands to benefit from it. The article goes on:
Perhaps that's why so few Canadians take full advantage of them. There is still an unrealistic, macho attitude around that says the man is supposed to have the money while the woman has the kids. Indulging that kind of attitude will cost you hundreds of dollars in taxes you don't really have to pay. For those of us who'd simply rather have more hard cash, here's some good news:
For a start, if you're earning about $30,000 and have the family house in your name, you're being about $500 unrealistic.
With a taxable income of about $30,000, your marginal tax rate-the rate charged on the last dollar you make-is 51 per cent, even if you live in Ontario (we shudder to think what it is in Manitoba). That means a $1,000 tax deferral will actually save you $500 in cash you will otherwise have to pay in taxes. That's $500 of real, extra cash in your pocket.
Here's the catch: that $1,000 deferral is available to you only if the family house is not in your name, nor held in joint tenancy, but is in your wife's name.
If you do not own a house now, you are entitled to deposit up to $1,000 a year for ten years in a registered home ownership savings plan. You are allowed to have only one of these plans in a lifetime. Once you have deposited for ten years, you are not entitled to make any further deposits.
But until then, your annual contribution is deductible for tax purposes. And, even better, you can get the money out tax free if you spend it to purchase a house, or to purchase furnishings or improvements to a house.
Those 10,000 tax-free dollars can be your down payment on a summer place. They can pay for the antique furniture you've always wanted. They can even give you a heck of a start at building that addition you've been planning to put on the back of the house. And while you're saving the $10,000, you're also saving $500 cash every year in income taxes. So-putting your house in your wife's name is worth about $500 a year. When you are old and gray and full of years, you'll pay a lot less in taxes if you are both drawing pensions.
The first $1,000 of annuity income from a registered pension plan at age 65 is tax-free. That's why it makes a lot of sense for you, as you are making deposits into a registered retirement savings plan, to make them not in respect of yourself, but in respect of your wife. The normal pension plan your employer operates has to be paid out to you. But an RRSP-whether it is a group RRSP at work, or a personal plan you are setting up-can provide a pension for your wife. The contributions to the plan are still deductible from your income for tax purposes. The limit on the size of your contribution-$3,500, less any moneys that you have been contributing to a company pension plan, or 20 per cent of your income-whichever is smaller-are the same if you are contributing to an RRSP for your wife as they are if you are contributing to your own plan. If you do not belong to a plan, the contribution limits are $5,500, or 20 per cent of income-whichever is smaller.
Setting up an RRSP for your wife can also provide you with some relatively short-term advantages. If she is not employed, she can draw the money out of the plan, and although she will be taxed on it when she draws it out, the total income in that year will be so small that the tax should be minimal. This is not to suggest that you can get into the habit of contributing to an RRSP for your wife every February 28th, and having her cash it in every March 1st. The contributions-like all transactions that have tax effects-must be genuine transactions.

Income Tax
But if a need for the money does arise, she can cash in the plan, and the money will be taxed at her rate-not yours.
The Department of National Revenue will depend on insurance companies, trust companies and banks to report withdrawals from the plan. I can just see them reporting that. I continue quoting:
But the real advantages of establishing pension income for your wife are at retirement. Then you will not only have two incomes-and therefore be taxed at a lower rate-but you will also have two pension income deductions of $1,000 each. The savings are really quite substantial.
The article continues:
Why settle for $1,000 worth of tax-free interest income when you could have more?
Your first $1,000 worth of interest income from Canadian sources is tax-free. Any interest costs you have to pay in order to earn this income-if, for instance, you borrow the money which you use to invest to earn interest-is also deductible against your income.
The same goes for your wife-and even better, if she earns some interest income, you are entitled to claim the rest of her $1,000 interest deduction against your income.
The next point is really interesting. I continue quoting the article:
Let's say you have $100,000 lying around the house. You decide to give it to your wife. She invests it at 10 per cent, and makes $10,000 on it in the first year. The attribution rules bring this income into your (the husband's) hands, and the $10,000 income is taxed at your rates. It's stacked on top of the other money earned and taxed at your marginal rate, not at hers. On the other hand, let's say you lend that $100,000 to your wife. You draw up a reasonable repayment schedule, have it notarized. She still invests it at 10 per cent, and still makes $10,000, but now the $10,000 is taxed in her hands, and at her lower marginal rate.
Like any transaction that has tax effects, the loan must be a real transaction. The Department of National Revenue had held that this means there must be a repayment schedule that is reasonable as part of the loan agreement, but there does not have to be an interest charge associated with the loan. And the loan has to involve money, not property. You can't lend your shares of Imperial Oil to your wife.
How big are the potential tax savings? Well, let's once again take an extreme case. Let's say your marginal rate is 50 per cent, and let's say the income that can be generated by the money you're going to lend to your wife is $10,000. If it is taxed in your hands, you'll be permitted to keep less than $5,000 of it (as your income climbs above $30,000, the marginal rate increases above 50 per cent). If you lend it to your wife, and it's her sole income, her taxes will be, at the most $3,000. Your minimum savings is $2,000.
The next point bears emphasizing:
If you work for yourself, it makes good sense for your wife to work for you too.
If you are a self-employed person, it may make sense to incorporate, and it will make good sense for you to employ your wife. The money you pay her will be money you don't need to run the household, and it will be money that will be taxed at her lower marginal rate rather than at your higher rate.
This doesn't mean that you can have your wife pick up the mail at your Post Office box every morning, and put her on the payroll at $25,000 a year. The income tax people stipulate that the salary you pay your wife must bear a reasonable relationship to her real contribution to the business. But even if you pay her only $1,000, and your marginal rate is 50 per cent, you have saved about $500 in income taxes.
On incorporation, you can make your wife a shareholder. She will then be in a position to draw dividend income from the company, and the dividend income can be reasonable-not in relation to her actual contribution to the company, but to its total earnings. This can have dramatic effects on the tax bite taken out of the money that is finding its way into your home.
Your wife's total income that year could be $13,000 in dividends. Her total tax liability will be zero. The company paid tax on the dividends coming out at
[Mr. Rodriguez.J
the small business tax rate, and it's better than increasing your income over the $25,000 amount.
Some serious questions arise in connection with these matters. I continue quoting:
What happens if, after I do all these things, my wife runs off with the milkman?
There are two answers to that.
The first is that, despite the escalating divorce rate, most marriages don't end in divorce.
The second answer is that planning your financial life as though your marriage were going to end that way is one of the worst possible ways to run a marriage. Personal financial consultants are often closely involved in marriage breakdowns. They say financial misunderstandings have put more marriages on the rocks than adultery ever has.
And that brings us to the big non-financial bonus you'll gain from making the kinds of income-splitting arrangements described here. You can't make them without talking to your wife about the family's real financial position. You can't make them without involving her. And the marriage counsellors we've talked to tell us that kind of mutual involvement in money matters is a great tonic for a marriage.
So forge ahead. Realizing what a great tax shelter your wife can be not only makes financial sense-it's good for the marriage, too.
So there you have it. I did not know that the government, instead of operating an income tax system, was really providing marriage counselling. It just shows you how you can get all screwed up in this place. We have made a comparison. Asking the Liberals to organize and be responsible for a tax system is like putting Count Dracula in charge of the Red Cross blood bank. We have often stated that opinion. This is again borne out in Bill C-22. So much for helping the homeowners and the wealthy in this country with the various kinds of finagling that can go on with the income tax system.
The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) said that the registered home ownership savings plan was established to help young couples save for a home. We subscribe to that. All members of this House, regardless of their ideology, recognize that there is a great need to assist young people who are today trying to save a nest-egg in order to be able to purchase a home. When that plan was introduced by the then minister of finance, who has now departed for the upper echelons of Bay Street, we held our criticism. We thought there were certain drawbacks, but we muted out criticism. On the surface at least there were some advantages to which everyone could subscribe. However, the plan is now being abused. When the plan was set up, loopholes were included in it. Is there no logical, fair-minded person in this House? I stated that the principles of our model of a tax system are redistributiveness, equity and progressivity. I challenge any member of this House to stand and say that the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan is fair.
I challenge you to sit down.
Hear, hear!

Is there any member of this House who thinks that the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan as presently constituted is fair and equitable? it is a tax haven, a
February 14, 1977

way for people to dodge their rightful responsibility to support this country. If every Canadian taxpayer took advantage of these programs, who would pay to keep this country going?
The poor people.

Yes, the poor people, the elderly people, as well as the miners in my area and those in Sault Ste. Marie, Timiskaming and Cape Breton. It is these people who pay the administration costs of government. Therefore, my plea today is for the little people of this country, the low wage earner, the disenfranchised.
I want to return to the registered retirement savings plan. That program is also abused. If this minister would stand and say that he is prepared to make changes that would plug the loopholes, we would immediately give our support. I would consider that a victory of sorts for the low income people of this country. However, I do not expect the minister to do that. He had his chance. The registered retirement savings plan is supposed to help thrifty people. No fair-minded person would say that is not a good idea. It is good that younger people are allowed to put money aside for their retirement. They should be able to write off that amount for income tax purposes. However, it is not designed to help thrifty people. It helps the wealthy in a very direct way, the wealthy who have extra income on which they do not want to pay tax. Therefore, this has become another tax shelter. That is our quarrel with these programs and the registered retirement savings plan in particular.
In 1974 there were 3,580,000 people in the $5,000 to $10,000 income bracket who recorded $123,471,000 in RRSP deductions, an average of $34.49 each. In contrast, there were 274,009 people in the $25,000 plus bracket who had an average deduction of $1,501.76.

He said: Mr. Speaker-

speechtext: Don't talk about income tax.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REQUIREMENT OF WITNESSES AT CORONERS' INQUESTS
speechtext:
Anything would be better now than income tax. The worst air disaster in the history of the Canadian Arctic occurred on October 30, 1974, when a Lockheed Electra transport plane crashed 2'A miles short of the landing strip at Rea point on Melville Island. Thirty-two men were killed as a result of the crash of the four-engine cargo-passenger aircraft which was owned and operated by Panarctic Oils Ltd. The aircraft was on a routine biweekly flight to change drilling crews at the site of one of Panarctic's operations. Three miles short of the landing strip, the plane was put into a nose-down position and power was reduced, thus increasing the rate of descent and making impact with the sea ice, far short of the runway, inevitable. Of the 34 passengers and crew on board the flight, 31 were killed immediately. The three survivors were exposed to a chill factor of some 75 degrees below zero Fahrenheit until they were rescued approximately two hours after the crash. The flight engineer, Gary Weyman, and the First ofFicer, David Hatton, survived the crash, but a passenger who had survived the initial impact died on the way to hospital in Edmonton. The cause of the crash was not immediately known.
OO)
Since October of 1974 the circumstances surrounding the accident have been subjected to three ofFicial investigations. The initial inquiry and inquest conducted under the authority of the coroner's ordinance of the Northwest Territories was one of those. Due to the limited powers of the inquest to establish the true facts of the crash, two subsequent investiga-

February 14, 1977
Inquests
tions were necessary. The Ministry of Transport conducted the investigation of the accident and Judge W. A. Stevenson was commissioned on November 20, 1975, to conduct an independent public inquiry into the circumstances surrounding the crash of the Lockheed Electra.
Only with the publication on June 29, 1976, of the evidence uncovered by the last inquiry was all the available information given to the public. It was a full 20 months after the accident before all relevant evidence was presented to the public. Relatives of the passengers killed in the crash, and relatives of the crew members, were left in a state of limbo during this time period. Civil suits were stalled and allegations and rumours concerning the captain of the Electra, Brian Thomson, were allowed to proliferate.
The prolonged time period between the actual crash and the release of the report of the independent inquiry was due to one further factor-the inability of the coroner, Mr. Walter England, to subpoena witnesses at the time of the inquest if their place of residence was outside the Northwest Territories. As a result, the two most important witnesses, the two survivors of the crash, were not in attendance at the inquest. Because the co-pilot and the flight engineer resided outside the Northwest Territories, and thus outside of the jurisdiction of the coroner, there was no way of compelling these men to attend. The jury was thus denied the best evidence available for determining what had caused the crash.
Section 21 of the Coroner's Ordinance of the Northwest Territories stipulates as follows:
A coroner may issue a summons in Form H respecting any person, who in his opinion, may be able to give material evidence at an inquest requiring him to appear at the time and place mentioned therein, to testify to all matters within his knowledge relating to the subject matter of the inquest and to bring with him and produce any document, book, paper or article that he has in his possession or under his control relative to the subject matter of the inquest.
While the powers outlined in the ordinance are extensive, and no doubt effective in most cases where witnesses are residents of the Northwest Territories or provinces, depending on where the inquest is held they are useless in terms of compelling the presentation of evidence from witnesses who normally reside outside the area of the inquest in this case. With respect to the Panarctic crash, the limited jurisdiction of the coroner entirely frustrated the inquest. The two survivors were both in the cockpit of the aircraft at the time of the crash and could have provided the jury with important information concerning the last two minutes before the crash.
Up until the last two minutes the plane had been in a normal descent pattern. At a point approximately three miles from its destination the aircraft, which had been travelling some 300 feet above sea level and 250 feet above the Rea Point airport, went into an abrupt descent and struck the sea ice. It broke up on impact, with the bulk of the craft ultimately breaking through the ice. The jury, however, was denied a first-hand account of the pilot and crew's actions and reactions during the last two critical minutes of that flight. In addition to the two crash survivors, several employees of Panarctic Oils Limited refused to testify at the inquest and could not be subpoenaed to attend the coroner's inquest because they were

outside the coroner's jurisdictional boundaries. Important background information concerning the procedural operations and regulations of both the Rea Point airport and Panarctic Oils Limited was thus unavailable to the jury.
The lack of jurisdictional authority of a coroner's inquest is, or should be, a matter of general concern to all Canadians. In this particular instance the type of plane involved is commonly used all over the country. If there had been some defect in it or in the way it is commonly operated which contributed to this disaster, the Canadian public had a right to know about it within a shorter period of time than 20 months. The north, in particular, depends upon air transportation and the people of the north should be able to have some confidence in the safety of their air transportation.
Further, this was one of the few occasions when members of a turbo-prop or a jet plane's flight crew survived a crash. Their testimony as to what happened in the last few moments was potentially of great value in preventing similar tragedies in the future. The Panarctic disaster clearly indicates the need for legislation making it possible to compel the attendance of witnesses at an inquest, even if they live without the boundaries of the province or territory concerned. Since coroners come under provincial jurisdiction, this would probably require legislation by all provinces, a thing not always easy to achieve. But it is surely in the interests of every province that an inquest investigating a crime or an accident anywhere in Canada should be able to get the evidence that it needs.
For more than a year after the accident public suspicion and ignorance surrounding the incident remained unanswered and undealt with. This situation could have been avoided if the jurisdictional authority at the initial inquest had been broader. Despite the competence of the jurors, they were unable to arrive at a conclusive interpretation of the events leading up to the crash. Realizing their inability to gather all the evidence, the jury recommended that a federal inquiry be set up to investigate the crash. It is also significant that one of the jury's 14 recommendations was that the powers of the coroner be broadened to enable him to subpoena witnesses from anywhere in Canada.
Despite the evident need for a public investigation, the government stalled and delayed the establishment of an independent public inquiry. Frustrated and concerned with this inaction on the part of the government, I rose in the House of Commons on July 25, 1975, as recorded at page 7935 of Hansard to ask the then minister of transport, Mr. Marchand, the following question:
Will the minister request that another inquiry be sought in Alberta so that the co-pilot and flight engineer may be subpoenaed to attend and this whole matter can be cleared up?
Mr. Marchand, the minister at that time, replied to the effect that he was studying the question and would give me an answer at a later date.
During the same summer, my hon. friend from Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) also questioned the then minister of
February 14, 1977

transport as to whether he would establish an independent inquiry into the accident. Mr. Marchand was evasive in his reply and would offer no commitment that an inquiry would be launched. Still there was no action on the part of the government. Realizing that it was choosing to ignore pleas from the House of Commons, I issued a press release in August of 1975 in the hope that the public, once made aware of the situation, would pressure the government into taking action. Finally, on November 20, 1975, Judge William Stevenson of Edmonton was ordered by the government to conduct a full public inquiry into the crash.
The delay in setting up the inquiry can only be regarded as irresponsible. Mechanisms for carrying out a full inquiry were available to the federal government which alone had the jurisdictional authority to summon witnesses regardless of their place of residence in Canada. Yet the inquiry was consented to only after substantial pressure from both within and outside the House of Commons.
The reluctance of the federal government to establish a full inquiry highlights the need for joint action on the part of the federal government, the Northwest Territories and the ten provinces to broaden the subpoena powers of coroners. In this case it would have been more efficient, and much less heartbreaking, for the relatives of those killed in the crash if the initial inquiry had been able to assemble and analyse all the evidence. As it was, relatives of those killed in the crash were still trying to obtain death certificates for the victims a year and one-half after the accident. Settlement of estates was held up because of the unavailability of death certificates. When they did become available, some relatives were forced to travel to the coroner's office in Yellowknife and pay a fee in order to obtain them. As a result of the circumscribed nature of the coroner's power of subpoena, three inquiries were necessary and 20 months had to pass before the facts were known to the public.
The minister of justice, on November 3, 1975, acknowledged the feasibility of action to extend the jurisdiction of coroners. In reply to a question from the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), he stated:
The solution to that problem is the enactment by the provinces of a uniform reciprocal recognition of subpoenas as was recommended a year ago by the uniformity commissioners. I urge provincial attorneys general to consider that report carefully and to act upon it. I would be happy at my meeting with the provincial attorneys general to raise this issue with them.
A co-ordinated effort on the part of federal, provincial and territorial authorities is essential to a successful attempt to extend the subpoena power of coroners. I strongly urge the federal government to take the initiative in bringing the necessary provincial and territorial officials together so that they can agree upon the means of changing existing coroners' ordinances. While it is clear that the subject falls under provincial jurisdiction, this is an obvious case where the federal government must accept its role as co-ordinator and urge the officials involved to consider the matter.
It was imperative from the beginning that the true story of the Panarctic crash be made known to the public, and it was extremely unfortunate that the facts were so long in coming to
Inquests
light. It was not until June 29, 1976, that Judge Stevenson revealed that the immediate cause of the accident was the action of the crew. Judge Stevenson held that captain Thomas's incapacitation was probably attributable to a cerebral seizure, and his conclusion that there had been a physical malfunction on the part of the captain relieved concern about the airworthiness of Panarctic's Lockheed Electra.
Aircraft are essential in the north to many of our activities. The numbers of flights are increasing substantially each year. Looking at the statistics, one sees that at Yellowknife and Inuvik the number of flights have more than doubled in a five-year period. It becomes imperative that the situation to which I have referred be looked into. Also, I regard the establishment of an independent inquiry commission to investigate transport accidents within federal jurisdiction as a crucial priority.
The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forre-stall) has introduced a private member's bill to this effect, and I strongly hope that members on both sides will lend their support to this legislation. As outlined in the explanatory note to Bill C-220, the commission would have exclusive but selective authority as against any other federal body to investigate all accidents resulting in death, injury or property loss occurring on any means of transportation under federal authority. Such a commission would help avoid conflicts of interest arising in cases where transportation accidents are investigated by the federal body which is responsible for making and enforcing the rules under which the transportation system operated when the accident occurred.
In conclusion, I should like to reiterate the importance of taking action to extend the power of subpoena enjoyed by coroners. Only when such broader powers have been conferred can Canadians be confident that all the evidence needed for a proper inquest will be presented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger) for moving this motion today. It is one which should receive the full attention of both this House and the government, and I hope today's debate will result in action on the part of the government.
The problem which the hon. member has outlined with particular reference to the Panarctic inquest has brought the circumstances into focus. It is one which has existed for a long time, however. From time to time accidents take place involving people from different provinces. Inquests are held, and while attendance at those inquests is often arranged voluntarily, from time to time this is not possible and testimony which is vital to a fair conclusion is missing. The basic difficulty is that there is at the moment no power to compel attendance of prospective witnesses who are outside the province or territory in which the inquest is being held.
The Supreme Court of Canada has held in a recent case, Faber v. The Queen, 1976, that a coroner's inquest is not
3024

February 14, 1977
Inquests
criminal in nature, but civil. Accordingly, there is no federal jurisdiction with respect to the compelling of attendance by witnesses at coroners' inquests. At present, civil rules of procedure in each province empower a provincial court to issue a commission to take the testimony of a person or persons resident out of the province if this testimony is deemed necessary for a civil suit within that province. This, however, is the kind of process which is subject to many delays. It is not the sort of legal process which you would want to have in order to obtain the evidence of witnesses while their memory of an incident or of an accident is fresh in their minds.
It is essential for the efficacy of the inquest procedure that witnesses come before the inquest as soon as possible after the accident. There has been a move in Canada to achieve uniformity, and the uniform law conference has recommended a draft interprovincial subpoena act. I understand that this legislation has been adopted in Manitoba, British Columbia, Newfoundland and the Northwest Territories. Although the model act does not contain provisions per se subpoenaing witnesses to coroners' inquests, it nevertheless contains sufficient flexibility to allow the law to be amended to include that kind of proceeding as well as proceedings before bodies other than normal court bodies. It is this sort of approach which, I am convinced, will produce the kind of result which the hon. member is seeking in advancing this motion today.
Since I am strongly in favour of what he is suggesting, I do not want to hold up the proceedings any further. I urge the government to listen to what has been said today, and I urge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to include this question on the agenda of his next meeting with provincial ministers of justice, to push for the adoption of the suggested draft interprovincial subpoena act of the uniform law conference, and to urge that this act include the flexibility necessary to permit the subpoenaing of witnesses not only to coroner's inquests but also before other bodies.
