I am interested in it because obviously we will have to do something about navigational aids and the assistance provided in those areas. Again, in that case, the Department of Transport is running interference for everyone. Information that had come out at the inquest is not available now, and the reports are secret. A couple of private reports are not available. It seems to me that information produced at an inquest should be right out in the open and the Department of Transport should not run interference for de Havilland aircraft

company or the manufacturer of the particular machine. Yet that appears to be the case. They either protect the insurance companies or they protect the companies which manufacture the aeroplanes. The right questions should be asked at an inquest, and the people who can answer those questions should be available, whether they are from the Northwest Territories or any other province. Anything else is totally unsatisfactory.
This afternoon I was discussing the safety factor with a couple of gentlemen who told me that a number of inquests had been held in that area but the reports that were made do not cover a number of important aspects. In both cases there were fatalities and both cases involve aluminum wiring. Everyone knows that aluminum wiring is dangerous and causes fires. The CSA in this country is powerful enough to involve interest groups, but they make no recommendations for a change. In fact, the people who make recommendations at inquests are not the people who should be called. They are the people who protect vested interests.
Three young people died in Ottawa as a result of the use of aluminum wiring. It is difficult to provide a proper connection on aluminum wiring for a single reason which is well documented and pictures are available showing what happens. The fire marshall at the coroner's inquest co-operated with vested interests to ensure that people did not get to the root of the problem. In my opinion the coroner's inquest is not the place where blame should be assessed. That can be done in civilian courts.
In the case of the accident in the Northwest Territories, it is difficult to see what the reason for the accident was because in my opinion there has been insufficient investigation and not enough information made available to enable the coroner's jury to reach a decision. The same was true in the Moosonee area accident in which a number of senior hydro officials and of band 9 council members were killed. It was also true in Sudbury where an inquest was called after a man had been killed and the union charge was that the working place was unsafe. INCO then went in and blasted the rock, thus getting rid of the site. When the jury wanted to look at it, it no longer existed. So it was all right for them to destroy the site, it was all right for them to eliminate all the fixtures in the electrical system which may have caused the fire, and it was all right in the case of the air crashes to make the people who were operating that equipment unavailable. But it is a hell of a way to provide justice. It is a hell of a system.
We should be allowed to find out exactly what happened; the information should be available at the inquest, and the chips should fall where they may. However, in all cases those people will probably end up sitting on coroners' juries making recommendations to prevent accidents, fires or fatalities from other causes in the future.
In a democratic system eliminating the problems we know about is the responsibility of everyone, and I hope that the passing of this motion this afternoon will mean that some of

the problems connected with coroners' juries and in connection with bringing witnesses before coroners will be solved.

speechtext:
So did the hon. member for Grenville-Carle-ton (Mr. Baker). In any event, there are a few short notes I would like to put on the record.
Legislative jurisdiction with respect to coroners' inquests is provincial or territorial, as the case may be, and not federal. Coroners in the territories have the power under territorial ordinances to subpoena witnesses, and this works well so long as the witnesses are in the jurisdiction. However, if the witnesses are somewhere else, there is no way for the coroner to compel them to appear. He just does not have jurisdiction outside the geographical area for which he is appointed. This problem is not unique to the Northwest Territories or the Yukon; coroners appointed under provincial statutes have the same problem.
The problem in the Northwest Territories came into sharp focus about two years ago in connection with the crash of a Panarctic airplane on October 30, 1974. Thirty-two people died in that crash, but two crew members survived. When the coroner was conducting his inquest, he naturally wanted to have the two surviving crew members attend to give evidence. They were outside the Northwest Territories and refused to go to the inquest. The eventual result was that the federal government, on the recommendation of the then minister of justice, appointed a judge under the Inquiries Act to conduct an inquiry into the crash, and under the Inquiries Act the judge had jurisdiction throughout the whole of the country, quite unlike the coroner, and he was able, therefore, to obtain all the necessary testimony.
The problems which arose in connection with the Panarctic inquest demonstrated how important was an earlier recommendation of the Uniform Law Conference of Canada. That conference, which was composed of provincial, territorial and federal government representatives, adopted in 1974 a uniform interprovincial subpoena act. This uniform act provided for a procedure for compelling the appearance of witnesses located
Inquests
outside the territorial jurisdiction of the relevant province or territory. This act was intended to apply not only to ordinary courts but also to subpoenas issued by coroners.
At the time of the Panarctic inquiry the Department of Justice suggested to the officials of the government of the Northwest Territories that they consider having discussions with provincial officials with a view to all jurisdictions enacting the uniform interprovincial subpoena act so that there could be procedures for compelling the attendance of witnesses who are outside the jurisdiction of each territory and province, and so that the statute could apply to coroners and to subpoenas issued by coroners. The officials of the Northwest Territories were very interested and attended at the very first opportunity to take up the matter with the provincial governments.

speechtext:
The hour appointed for the consideration of private members' business having expired, I do now leave the chair until eight o'clock.
At 5.40 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-22, to amend the statute law relating to income tax, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying in my few remarks before private members' hour this afternoon, the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan is one aspect of the tax system that we, on this side of the House, believe provides more than one tax loophole for people who participate in the program in certain ways.
During the supper hour 1 was visited by a friend who described a new wrinkle to the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. The more I hear about this program the more I am convinced it must have more ways than Masters and Johnson in its application.
Who is Masters and Johnson?

The hon. member knows who Masters and Johnson are. Here is a new wrinkle. A man and a woman, married, buy a home at the beginning of January and put it in her name. Then he establishes a Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan and for five years pays $1,000 each year into it. At the end of the five years it has accumulated interest and there is about $6,000 in it. At that point her mortgage comes up for review.
What does she do? She sells him part ownership in the home, for which he pays her $6,000. She then goes down to the bank; it is review time for the mortgage and she puts $6,000 against the outstanding mortgage. And, voila, what is the
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
result? The Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan is prostituted again. That is a new wrinkle. There is nothing illegal about it. But that is the kind of thing we have tried to draw to the attention of the House.
If time had permitted, we would have driven home these points to the minister and done our best to obtain changes in Bill C-22. It is my job to draw attention to clauses of the bill to which we object. We must bring home the injustice of this particular clause to the majority of taxpayers in Canada who cannot afford to take advantage of that kind of loophole.
Peter Myers wrote in the Ottawa Citizen of December 6, 1976, that the RHOSP is amazingly generous. It helps people who expect to buy homes in the future, families who want summer cottages, and even couples who are quite satisfied with their homes already. But like the other deductions, the wealthy benefit way more than low income earners. As I shall show, the facts bear out the truth of this contention.
For those earning less than $2,000 the average amount of grant was $105.21; for those earning between $2,000 and $5,000, the amount of grant was $203.18; for those earning between $5,000 and $10,000, the amount of grant was $264.93; for those with incomes between $10,000 and $15,000, it was $309.93. Those earning between $15,000 and $20,000 received grants of $365.80. For those with incomes between $20,000 and $50,000 the amount of grant was $462.11, and for those with incomes exceeding $50,000, it was $571.06. Those facts clearly show that the rich are getting richer. People at the bottom of the income scale for whom, presumably, the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan was designed and who have the greatest need, got peanuts.
As we have tried to show in this debate, our model of the tax system is based on three principles: first, the redistributive principle; second, the equity principle; and third, the progress-ivity principle. I do not know if anyone in the House can tell me if this measure which we are debating is based on any of those three principles, or on all of them. In our minds there is no question but that the kinds of loopholes we have been discussing permit high income earners in this country to avoid paying their fair share of taxes which are needed to support the country, and programs which are absolutely necessary if there is to be stability and equity for the people of this country.
We are not alone in our opinion. It is echoed by the National Council of Welfare. Incidentally, the head of that council turned down an opportunity to sit on the Tory policy advisory committee. I find that extremely interesting. That council can by no means be described as a group of left-wing radicals, and this is what it says. I quote:
Imagine a minister responsible for housing announcing a new program of federal-provincial grants intended to encourage home ownership. These grants would vary by a person's income.
Of course such a program is unthinkable. The idea of a grant that increases with income would cause a furor in parliament and among the public. A minister of housing who would suggest such a program in the privacy of a cabinet meeting would be laughed out of the room-not to say out of the cabinet.
However a former finance minister announced just such a program in the November 1974 budget and it became law. The program is called the Registered
February 14, 1977

Home Ownership Savings Plan-another of the savings incentives built into the Income Tax Act.
The purpose of Registered Home Ownership Savings Plans is "to assist young people in accumulating the capital required for a down payment on a house." One could wonder how many young people are in the income groups that derive the substantial benefits. It is certainly interesting to note that among persons making between $5,000 and $10,000 a year, only one in 49 took advantage of this provision. In the income range between $10,000 and $15,000, one in 32 opened up a plan. However in the $50,000 or more income group, the figure was one in 16.
I will not belabour the point. It is obvious, according to the National Council of Welfare and other statistics which have been quoted, that the wealthy are overwhelmingly taking advantage of this generous program. One in 16 of those earning more than $50,000 a year has taken advantage of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan.
The loopholes under the plan are indeed lucrative. As I have shown, the plan can be prostituted in all sorts of ways. I draw attention in this regard to the homeowners' dodge whereby many have transferred their property to the wife's or husband's name and taken a tax deduction for a contribution to a Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan. For example, if a man's income is higher than his wife's he might use the scheme as a handy way of saving taxes while at the same time building up a tax-sheltered fund. Any interest earned by this fund is tax free. If the taxpayer contributed $1,000 for ten years at 8 per cent annual interest, the fund would build up to $15,645. A taxpayer in a 30 per cent tax bracket for the top portion of his income would save $300 a year in taxes. If this $300 were invested at 8 per cent per annum, it would amount to nearly $4,700 in ten years. Thus, by contributing $1,000 a year for ten years a nest egg of more than $20,000 would be accumulated.
As I said, one partner in a marriage can become eligible by selling his or her share of a home to the other partner. The share would be sold by the partner with the higher income, who can make the best use of the RHOSP. The tax-free savings can be used to buy a second home or even-imagine this-to buy back the same home from the partner who owns it. That is a new wrinkle. I know that the minister can get up in this House and say, with the help of his charts and Figures, that X percentage of the people have done this or done that. We know that the program is available to any Canadian who can afford to take advantage of it. Unfortunately, few are able Financially to take advantage of the program. Therefore it is not used for the purpose for which it was designed. It has become a tax dodge.
Not long ago I asked, rhetorically, that if every single Canadian were to take advantage of the RHOSP program which I have described, and take advantage of the RRSP, who would bear the tax burden for those other programs which our country needs and which must be supported? How many would bear the burden? There would be very few people. We know who they are. As was pointed out this afternoon, it would be the poor people and the pensioners who would probably carry the burden.
Income Tax
Let us look at the twin program of the RHOSP, and the RRSP. Let us look at the benefits of the Registered Retirement Savings Plan.
That is important.

The hon. member says it is important. It is very important. This party has talked about a national pension scheme for a long time. What do we get? We get the Canada Pension Plan. I recognize that the buddies of the government are in the insurance companies and banks of Bay Street. The government would not want to challenge them on that. It would mean taking away a very lucrative business.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) now wants to fight with the banks. He still has not paid for his airplane trip to Toronto. I want to know why not. That is important, especially when we are dealing with banks, their power, and the way they calculate interest on the savings of Canadians.
The Registered Retirement Savings Plan is supposed to help thrifty people put money away for their retirement.
Only rich thrifty people; poor thrifty people do not have any money.
I wish the hon. member would not talk like that about the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pig-gott). She is just a poor little person.
Here is a present for you.

It isn't ticking, Mr. Speaker. I think I am being bribed. Some people will do anything to get me to close my mouth and sit down. The hon. member has presented me with some cookies. This would be more appropriate for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: He eats only Arrowroot.
I baked them myself.
She thinks there's something crummy about you.
I will not be swayed, Mr. Speaker. I will not be bribed.
You just were.
I always wanted to get my hands into the hon. member's cookie jar.
Watch it. This has been a clean debate so far.

Well, she has a cookie jar in her office.
Getting back to the Registered Retirement Savings Plan, this was supposed to help thrifty people put money away for

February 14, 1977
Income Tax
their retirement. However, it only helps wealthy people who have extra money they do not want taxed.
In 1974 there were 3,850,000 people in the $5,000 to $10,000 income bracket. They recorded $123,471,000 in RRSP deductions. That is an average of only $34.49 each. In contrast, 274,009 people in the $25,000 plus bracket had an average deduction of $1,501.76, for a grand total of $411,470,000 in excess income socked away. That is absolutely incredible.
The income tax system is supposed to be progressive. It is supposed to redistribute wealth in this country. A former finance minister, who has gone to his reward on Bay Street, opened up these loopholes for his wealthy friends. What is fair and just when those in the average and low income bracket have a saving of approximately $34.49 in contrast to the $1,501.76 for those in the $25,000 plus bracket? It is obvious that we have a big "L" government. With those odds, the poor people lose.
I wish to quote from an article that appeared in the Financial Post "How Savings Grow in Tax Sheltered RRSP". I quote:
This example compares with the accumulation of savings achieved through annual contributions to an RRSP and through a fund produced from after-tax income.
It assumes an individual can, from the age of 35 on, afford to put aside $1,000 a year from pre-tax income for retirement. The effect of assuming a 50 per cent marginal tax rate throughout the period and a 40 per cent rate are compared. Obviously the higher the tax rate, the greater the advantage of tax-sheltering contributions and the interest earned. Annual interest of 7 per cent is assumed throughout the period.
With an annual investment of $1,000 in an RRSP at the 50 per cent marginal tax rate, in ten years a person would have accumulated $14,784. After 30 years, he would have accumulated $101,073. Obviously this plan is not designed for low income Canadians.
Jerry Beaulieu works 60 hours a week in a cold and wet carwash in Toronto. He earns $8,650 a year. There is no way that Jerry Beaulieu can save $1,000 a year to put into an RRSP. Can you imagine Jerry Beaulieu in his overalls and rubber boots walking into that stable establishment called the Royal Bank and saying that he wants to borrow $1,000?
Only if he had a gun in his hand.

Yes, and we know how far he would get with that. Jerry Beaulieu's tax saving would be nothing compared to a tax saving of $470 that is possible for Lloyd Robertson who earns $100,000 a year. I imagine Lloyd Robertson could get by putting his $1,000 a year into an RRSP and getting a $470 tax saving. However, Jerry Beaulieu who works in that dank, damp carwash in Toronto for 60 hours a week and earns $8,650 could not take advantage of that program. Obviously the plan was designed for the friends of the boys in Ottawa.
We should keep in mind the real purpose of the RRSP. We are reasonable people here. I am fairly reasonable. The RRSP was touted as an opportunity for people to put away money for

their retirement years. However, it has been prostituted. The loopholes are so large that elephants can walk through them. And so the RRSP has degenerated and become a tax dodging device for high income earners.
They even advertise that.

Yes, that is the way they advertise them, Mr. Speaker. One has only to look at the great scramble on the part of banks, trust companies and insurance companies whose advertising is designed to get you to put your money into RRSP's. Their advertisements say: "See by how much you can avoid paying the tax man"; "Avoid the tax grab"; and so on ad nauseam. I do not think that that sort of thing is fair to the rest of the taxpayers of this country. I do not think it is fair to the 16,000 hourly rated employees of INCO. I do not think it is fair to people who work for wages on an hourly basis and who are in no position economically to take advantage of these kinds of loopholes and tax dodges. Suddenly the RRSP is the magic formula for escaping taxes and making money to boot.
I could not escape the horrendous ad campaign being conducted in the Toronto subway, which I saw the other day when I was there. There in blazing colour was an ad which read:
How to make money make money.
Start turning your nest egg into a golden future by March 1st.
Both National Trust's 9 per cent "no charge"
RHOSP and National Trust's "high interest"
RRSP will help your money make money.
It's a golden opportunity.
Just walk by any trust company's office, Mr. Speaker, and you will be confronted with similar ads.
Here is another example which I extracted from the Globe and Mail for Tuesday, February 8, 1977. In big black letters was an ad from Credit Foncier reading:
There's more to your RRSP and RHOSP than tax savings.
The tax savings offered by all financial institutions, including Credit Foncier Trust, are identical. That's established by law. The key features you should focus on in choosing your Registered Retirement or Home Ownership Savings Plans are: Security, High Return, Flexibility No Sales or Administration Fees.
And on and on it goes, Mr. Speaker. This is the kind of advertising which is geared toward the people who have the money to invest. Unfortunately it is not the kind of advertising that opens the door to people like Jerry Beaulieu and so many people across the country who earn less than $ 10,000 a year.
The loopholes in the law are incredibly glaring. They are so glaring that Revenue Canada is now concerned about tracking down and closing the loopholes and threatening to prosecute, but they say they cannot, that their hands are tied by the legislation. All the minister had to do when this bill was at report stage was to stand up in this House and announce that he would accept amendments to block these glaring loopholes which permit the tax system of Canada to be used as a rip-off, rather than as a means of collecting tax and redistributing the tax in a fair and progressive manner.
February 14, 1977

As I have said, the loopholes in the RRSP are incredibly glaring, and I have already mentioned a few of them. But there are more. Here is another article by that famous tax lawyer whom I have been quoting incessantly since last Monday because he is an intriguing person. He is Mr. Paul Dioguardi and he writes in the Ottawa Citizen. He has more positions in regard to using this plan than the happy hooker. He headlines his article "Retirement Savings Plan Can Be a Tax-Saving Tool Too," and the article is as follows:
Although the Registered Retirement Savings Plan has been around since 1957, its potential as a tax saving tool has usually not been fully realized. Some time ago an interesting paper covering some of the possible benefits from RRSPs was presented before an annual meeting of the Canadian Tax Foundation.
The first point examined dealt with a spousal RRSP, the second with deductible mortgage interest. In both cases, the paper used tax deductible contribution limits before the 1976 federal budget. Calculations, therefore, are not exact and are presented here for illustrative purposes only.
Our hypothetical taxpayer-let's call him John Q. Taxpayer-is married, has no registered pension plan and is in a 50 per cent tax bracket. He contributes $4,000 each year for five years to his wife's RRSP. Each year the $2,000 he saved by being able to take a tax deduction on the RRSP contribution is used to fund a portion of the contribution.
The remaining $2,000 comes from liquidating some of his income-producing investments which he later repurchases with borrowed funds. (This is necessary because interest on money borrowed to make a contribution to a spouse's RRSP is not deductible.)
At the end of the five-year period the spousal RRSP is collapsed. The value of the assets in the plan, assuming that they have been invested at 9 per cent interest compounded annually, would be $23,940.
It is then necessary to take into consideration the amount of tax which would have to be paid when the money is withdrawn from the plan. This can be set at $7,223 using 1975 tax rates and assuming that the wife has no other income in the payout year.
In addition, one must compute the tax on the lost spouse exemption in the year in which the funds are paid out. This comes to about $822 leaving a net amount in hand, before loan payments, of $15,895.
Mr. Taxpayer then must pay the bank for the $2,000 loans taken out each year. Assuming a tax deductible rate of interest of 10 per cent, his payout would be in the area of $ 11,500.
After working out the mathematics, it can readily be seen that Mr. Taxpayer could have realized, as a result of these transactions, a net profit of $4,395. (The result would be even better using the new $5,500 contribution limit.)
That is proposed in this bill.
Naturally tax savings are more dramatic when using the example of a person in a 50 per cent tax bracket, but the procedure may also be of interest to those at lower tax levels.
Assuming Mr. Taxpayer is a participant in a registered pension plan and has the ability, within the deductibility limitations imposed by the Income Tax Act, to contribute $1,200 each year to a spousal RRSP.
If he had a taxable income in the $ 14,700 range each year and follows the drill previously outlined his tax saving would be slightly more than $1,000.
A spousal plan is not the only way an RRSP can be used to save tax dollars. Another concept utilizes an RRSP to effectively convert part of a taxpayer's home mortgage interest expense into tax deductible interest. It goes something like this:
Assume our friend Mr. Taxpayer has a $30,000 mortgage on his home. It comes up for renewal every five years and there are four more years to run on the mortgage.
For some time he's been making annual contributions of $4,000 to his RRSP. These amounts have not been borrowed and, therefore, over the next four years he will have invested $16,000 in the RRSP out of his free cash.
If he could utilize the $16,000 free cash to pay down the mortgage and then increase the mortgage in order to fund the RRSP contribution, it should be possible to make the interest on the $16,000 mortgage liability tax deductible.
Income Tax
Instead of using his own money to contribute to the RRSP, Mr. Taxpayer borrows $4,000 from the bank and makes his RRSP contribution from these funds. The $4,000 of his own free cash is then invested in Canada Savings Bonds or other easily cashable securities which pay good interest rates.
For each of the next three years, Mr. Taxpayer follows the same procedure until he has accumulated a bank debt of $16,000 and a bond investment of the same amount.
The only cost he should incur would be the spread between the interest paid to the bank and that received from the bonds. When the mortgage becomes due he simply cashes in the bonds and pays it down by $16,000.
Then he increases his mortgage by $16,000 and uses this additional money to pay off the bank loan.
Mr. Taxpayer is now in a position to claim a deduction of the mortgage interest on $16,000 because that amount was borrowed in order to pay off a bank loan which was originally used for the tax deductible purpose of contribution to an RRSP.
Although both of these alternatives may be of some interest, taxpayers should be cautious in tailoring their tax planning to fit the particular situation. Otherwise the result could be financially unpleasant.
Looking through this proposal, Mr. Speaker, one can readily conclude that it is not lower income Canadians who would be able to profit from the kind of advice which people like Mr. Dioguardi are able to provide with respect to investments in connection with the RRSP program.
We in the New Democratic Party are also completely and unconditionally opposed to clause 65. This clause is one in connection with which we requested extra time for discussion, because at the time the debate at the report stage ended only some two and one-half or three minutes had been spent on clause 65. This clause means that the surtax on high income earners will be in effect only for 1976. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has confirmed that it will not be continued notwithstanding the fact that it was part of the anti-inflation program which is continuing beyond 1976. What a flip-flop!
Back in December, 1975, the Minister of Finance made the following remarks in the House of Commons:
As the House is well aware, it has been our concern from the beginning that the anti-inflation program should be fair, and should be seen to be fair, to all groups in our economy. That is critical to the credibility of the program and crucial to its success.
He went on to say:
In terms of fairness and equity, it is, we believe, only fair that those at the upper end of the income scale, who are able to absorb the impact of rising living costs without undue hardship, should be asked to shoulder some share of the burden ... We have come to the conclusion that a surtax should be levied on all those in the upper income bracket whether they be professionals, independent businessmen, corporate executives, well-to-do farmers or senior public servants. While the guidelines do provide for a maximum increase of $2,400, it is fair to ask those who already enjoy ample means to make a proportionately greater sacrifice in the national interest.
So much for equal sacrifices. But what is to be expected? The minister, when he introduced the surtax at the time of the anti-inflation program, said that those in the higher tax brackets had to bleed a little. Yet, here, under clause 65 he said the tax is being lifted.

Boring!

Income Tax

You may say it is boring, but there goes the credibility of the government. This tax was introduced along with the government anti-inflation program. It is all right for you to laugh over there, but your turn will come.
What could we expect? The Anti-Inflation Board did not seem to affect Eric Trigg, executive vice-president of Alcan Aluminum, whose salary in the first year of the program went from $147,348 to $162,178, an increase of 10 per cent. Nor did affect John Armstrong, chairman of the board and president of Imperial Oil, whose salary jumped $30,000 in the first year of the program. The elimination of the surtax after 1976 is just another concession to the wealthy in Canada. The tax saving for someone in the $50,000 income bracket will be $402. For someone in the $80,000 bracket, clause 65 will mean a saving of $1,654, and for someone earning $100,000 it will mean $2,491. In total, it will cost the treasury, in other words, the people of Canada, $135 million, and every penny of it will go to the 2 or 3 per cent of Canadians with incomes of $30,000 plus. Is there anyone in the House who will tell me that this is an equitable tax system?
Clause 65 grants substantial savings to the wealthy, savings which are additional to the benefits these groups have reaped by escaping controls through the use of regressive tax measures such as personal income tax indexing and a variety of special tax shelters for high-income earners, shelters which make it doubtful that any individual would report a taxable income of $500,000.
The decision to rescind the surtax means that the burden shouldered by these income groups is being lifted at the time when the average working person is asked to accept stringent limits on wage increases. As far as this party is concerned, the only acceptable change in the application of the surtax would be to increase it.
We turn now to the question of indexing. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) is looking askance at me. I can see it in his eyes; he is asking me: am I going to get into this subject? Well, I will give that some thought, and in due course I will let him know.
He is not holding his breath.

I am not suggesting he should do so. The government whip says the observations made have not been profound. Well, he did not have much to say when we discussed this bill in committee. He was sheepish, almost seal-like in the way he sat waving his flippers, like a seal waiting for a fish. Now he is heckling from his place. I wish he had made his comments at a time when such remarks would have been appropriate. I turn, as I say, to the question of indexing.
It is no wonder the Liberal government is-in trouble. It is no wonder that poll after poll shows that the people are turning away in droves from the Liberal party. The bill before us is the most recent in the long line of mistakes the Liberal government has made. However, the interesting thing about the indexing system is to know where the Liberal government got it. Anyone looking at the income tax system would think that

indexing was thought up by the Liberal government, but the Conservatives have claimed credit for our indexing system.
It was in the minority period-I think in 1973 or 1974- when the government brought in indexing of tax exemptions. I think it was the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) who advocated it in the 1972 campaign. Lo and behold, the Liberals stole the indexing system from the Conservatives and put it into effect. However, that was not the only thing that was stolen from the Conservatives. The Liberals also stole wage and price controls, and we know what is happening in that regard. Another thing stolen from the Conservatives was the latest proposed change to the Unemployment Insurance Act, moving the minimum period of attachment from eight to 12 weeks.
Does it really matter who sits on the government benches, whether it be Tweedledee or Tweedledum? They steal from each other. I am glad the Liberals are now stealing from the Conservatives because that means that our programs can remain intact.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Such as they are.

Our programs can remain intact because they are waiting for the moment when socialism comes to the government of Canada. Hon. members will notice that in every instance when the government has taken a program from the official opposition-and indexing is one of these-it has been a dismal failure.
It is estimated that last year indexing cost Canada $1 billion in taxes.
Bay Street thinks that is great.

The boys on Bay Street think that is great. The fact is that the indexing in our income tax system allows the wealthy to get the best breaks. I was asked what our model for an income tax system would be, and I pointed out that our income tax system would embrace three principles. One is the principle of redistribution. We would want a system which would redistribute the taxes collected. Second, there would be the principle of equity, and third, the principle of progressivity.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You went into that an hour ago.
I have to repeat it for the Conservatives.
You have forgotten it already.
They have a short attention span; that is the difficulty. However, the indexing system permits the warp in the system to become even more pronounced.
Oh, oh!

The hon. member may ask a question at ten minutes to ten.
February 14, 1977

We have before us Bill C-22, and once again the government admits it stole the policies in this bill from the Conservative party. There is little doubt where these ideas came from, and if there is, it can be cleared up very quickly; all we have to do is ask any frontbencher in the Conservative party.
As we turn our attention to this bill, we see that it has cost the taxpayers $1 billion because of the indexing system. If we had taken $1 billion and used it in a creative manner with respect to tax credits, we could have done much to close the gap. We could have done much in terms of redistributing the wealth of the country and eliminating the massive poverty which plagues so many portions of our great country.
What does the government do when it is time to consider the tax system? It does not do the things the Carter Commission outlined. Time and again changes to the tax system have been suggested, but the government tinkers around with the works and comes up with indexing, and as a result the situation is made even more complicated than it was before.
Earlier I made reference to that great benefactor of the Canadian economy, that selfless corporation performing the big, top, expensive job, to use its own propaganda. If there is any doubt, I speak of Imperial Oil. Some hon. members present may be familiar with that corporation. Fewer still, I am sorry to say, are aware of the massive tax breaks it has received from this "just society".
In 1975, which is the last year for which statistics are available, Imperial Oil, the Rockefellers' gift to the Dominion of Canada, received $76 million in deferred taxes. Added to these benefits for corporations, the government refuses to close the tax loophole which permits multinational firms to set up foreign subsidiaries and then divert income out of Canada to lessen their tax liabilities. He headed a moderate party between the aristocratic conservative party of Pompey and the radical party of Julius Caesar. Yet, says Plutarch, he was "neither a steadfast friend nor an implacable enemy, but readily abandoned both his favours and his resentments at the dictates of his interests."
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, Marcus Crassus was a Liberal. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) says that Marcus Crassus piddled while Rome burned, but I do not know about that.
Sure gave them a hosing.

The Liberals are not the only ones who are indifferent to the problems created by the taxation system in Canada. The Tories are equally indifferent to income disparities and poverty in Canada. They care so much about inequality in Canada that they could not even find 30 seconds of time to say something good, bad or indifferent about Bill C-22 on third reading. This has resulted in my having to step into the breach and make this sacrifice of speaking to this bill in detail.
A glance at the Parliamentary Guide would reveal to all who care to look the great array of wealth among my hon. friends to the right of where I sit. Their interests range from the directorship of a management company and of an apartment company all the way to a fisheries company, a packing company, and a company making wheels, brakes and equipment. One gentleman is a banker. We have bakers, too, and candlestick makers. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) is fairly big in oil. Then, of course, there is the "Cookie Monster". And who can forget the generosity of the cookie monster? No one! I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and I are supplied with cookies enough for a lifetime.
Income Tax
It is certainly not surprising to note that the Tories have given their stamp of approval to Bill C-22. This is the party which thought the government had gone too far with tax reform in 1972. In fact the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) is quoted in the Globe and Mail of October 2, 1973, as having said:
Edgar Benson and Prime Minister Trudeau have offered too much reform in one step. Their reform could not be explained. They could not lead the country in any united, let alone trusting way, to a new system.
The Liberal party's so-called tax reform may be unexplainable and irrational, but the Tory idea of reform, which involves more tax reform commissions and more discussion, is so chicken-hearted that we can never expect anything beyond platititudes. If they are serious about tax reform, even in modest stages, why have we not heard a single concrete proposal from their benches during this debate? There has not been a squeak out of them. Like mice, they run for cover. They run under the desks and scare the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), who is afraid of mice, and ran out of the House.
The socialist party on this side of the House objects to such disparities in income and to too much poverty in one of the wealthiest countries of the world. The Prime Minister says he does not mind if the rich get richer as long as the poor get richer. The fact remains that, despite all supposed attempts by the government to redistribute income, the low-income groups are still receiving a lesser share of total income than during the mid sixties before many social welfare policies were improved.
We believe the income tax system must incorporate the ability-to-pay principle. We have said that in our view an income tax system must be based on three principles. It must be redistributive. It must be progressive. And it must be based on equity. Mr. Speaker, there is nothing in the present system which meets any of these principles.
This bill ought to be thrown out of the House of Commons along with the Liberals and their Tory buddies. We say the tax system must incorporate the ability-to-pay system. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, which income group pays the greater proportion of its earnings in taxes? Is it those in the upper brackets, those in the middle brackets, or those in the lower brackets? The answer is, those in the lower brackets. Some of my hon. friends have guessed it. They will get a cookie for that. People earning less than $8,000 pay the highest proportion of their total earnings in taxes. We also know, according to 1969 statistics, that 8.3 per cent of family units receiving an income of $15,000 paid at a rate amounting to 8.4 per cent less than those earning $2,000.
Here is another question. The top 20 per cent of Canadian income earners get 48 per cent of total income. How much do the bottom 20 per cent receive? Is it 15 per cent, or 3 per cent, or 8 per cent, or 12 per cent? The answer, Mr. Speaker, is 3 per cent.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker

No, no! Go on!

February 14, 1977
Income Tax

I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That", and by substituting therefor the following words:
"Bill C-22 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the
Committee of the Whole for the purpose of reconsidering Clause 65 thereof."
I place this motion before the House and trust that hon. members will support it.
I asked a question a moment ago. What is the answer? The answer is 3 per cent. It's the rich what gets the gravy, it's the poor what gets the blame.
